SCENE 2: Joseph's dream of the sheaves, Genesis 37. Seventeen-year-old Joseph sleeps peacefully on a simple bedroll in his family's open tent, head and face clearly visible low left, the same richly striped robe neatly folded beside him. In the upper and right half an unmistakable beautiful dream-vision blends naturally with the night sky: a sunlit wheat field with one upright tied sheaf in the centre while other tied sheaves bend toward it in a semicircle. The sheaves are real bundles of harvested wheat with stems and tied waists, NOT people or faces. A gently luminous dream transition separates the real sleeping boy from the dream wheat field without a cartoon thought-bubble outline. Moon-blue shadows and warm oil-lamp glimmer in the tent. Quiet wonder, not fantasy monsters. Large simple clear composition, Joseph is the emotional focal point.

SCENE 3: Joseph in the empty cistern, Genesis 37. View down obliquely into a broad shallow-looking ancient dry stone cistern so Joseph's full upper body and face are LARGE in the lower centre and readable, not a tiny silhouette far away. Seventeen-year-old Joseph wears plain cream linen with no colourful coat; he sits on dry sand and rounded stones, looking upward with fear and sadness but alert and unharmed. An opening to bright daylight at the upper part of the composition; two or three older brothers stand beyond the rim exchanging uncertain looks, one holding the familiar richly woven crimson/indigo/ochre coat. No violence in progress, no injuries, no chains, no water, no blood. A shaft of daylight reaches Joseph's face and hands to keep the plate printable and hopeful. Clear contrast between lonely boy below and brothers above, realistic rock geometry.

SCENE 4: Joseph taken toward Egypt with a trading caravan, Genesis 37. Large seventeen-year-old Joseph at the left foreground in a plain off-white tunic, walking in three-quarter view beside a mature trader, Joseph turns his face back toward the distant hills of home with longing. A small caravan of camels carrying woven packs follows a dusty path through a broad sunlit ancient landscape toward the right distance. A trader has a small purse of silver coins at his belt, but money is not the focal point. Joseph is being taken away and has no coloured coat; show him distressed but unharmed, no ropes round his neck, no beating or dramatic chains. Late afternoon warm dusty gold with blue distant hills, ample open space conveying distance and separation, authentic merchants, no modern roads. At most a few readable figures, no crowded market.

SCENE 5: Joseph in an Egyptian prison after an unjust accusation, Genesis 39-40. Large Joseph kneels at centre and offers a small clay cup of water to a seated, discouraged fellow prisoner, making gentle eye contact. A second prisoner sits nearby listening. Rough but plausible ancient Egyptian stone interior, straw mats, clay jug, simple wooden barred doorway in the background, a high window admits broad blue-gold daylight across the people's faces. They are confined but retain dignity. Emphasise Joseph's kindness and hope despite injustice, not torture or spectacle. No shackles, no scars, no violence, no sinister dungeon. Make the figures large, the emotional interaction clear, details restrained and printable.

SCENE 6: Pharaoh troubled by his dream, Genesis 41. An ancient Egyptian pharaoh, a realistic mature Egyptian man with brown skin, wearing a tasteful blue/gold striped royal headdress and white linen, sits suddenly upright on his simple elegant royal bed at the left foreground, looking troubled rather than terrified. An oil lamp lights his face and hand. Beyond him a soft, unmistakable dream-vision blends into the cool blue night: the banks of the Nile, reeds and TWO contrasting representative cows, one healthy and well-fed with a full rounded body, one very lean and bony but living and not gruesome. The pair symbolises the two herds in the seven-year dream; this is a selective visual dream detail, do not clutter the image trying to draw fourteen cows. Gentle hazy edges clearly show this is a dream, not cows inside the bedroom. Egyptian stone pillars and woven bed linen. No Joseph in this scene, no modern bedding, no hieroglyphic writing or subtitles. Cinematic twilight/oil lamp realism and a clear narrative contrast.

SCENE 7: Joseph explains the dream and proposes saving grain before Pharaoh, Genesis 41. Joseph, now about thirty, newly clean-shaven with the same recognisable dark curly hair and slim Levantine face, stands large at centre-left wearing clean simple white linen. He calmly gestures toward TWO large woven baskets before him: one filled with golden grain, the other empty, as a visual explanation of abundance followed by hunger. Pharaoh sits at right on a dignified ancient Egyptian wooden chair/throne with discreet gold decoration, blue/gold striped royal headcloth and white linen, listening intently with a thoughtful respectful expression. A single Egyptian attendant in the soft background. Joseph has no ceremonial collar yet: the focus is the wise plan, not a coronation. Spacious pillared ancient Egyptian palace, sunlit doorway toward green Nile fields, warm reflected sunlight on human faces, real stone and woven baskets. No charts, no speech bubbles, no parchment writing, no modern objects. Mutual respect and a hopeful turning point.

SCENE 8: The seven years of plenty, grain stored wisely in Egypt, Genesis 41. A third worker carrying a woven basket is in the middle distance, not a huge crowd. Golden grain visibly streams from the basket and a rich but believable store fills the chamber. SCENE 10: Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place after the silver cup is found, Genesis 44. In an Egyptian governor's reception room Joseph stands at right in his white linen and gold-and-turquoise official collar, clean-shaven with the same reference dark curly hair, moved and listening carefully. At left centre Judah, a recognisable older brother with brown beard streaked grey and a simple brown cloak, steps forward with an open earnest palm and his other hand protectively on Benjamin's shoulder. Benjamin is a YOUNG ADULT brother about twenty-five years old, dark curly hair, youthful light beard, pale linen tunic, worried but not hurt; he is not a little child. A plain silver drinking cup lies prominently on a folded grain sack between them, held by nobody, symbolising what has been found. One other brother stands behind Judah in solidarity. No armed guards, no chains, no violence. Judah's courage and willingness to stand by his younger brother is the focal point. Large faces and hands in a calm, legible horizontal composition, sun-warmed ancient stone and restrained palace detail.

SCENE 11: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers, Genesis 45. A deeply human reunion in the Egyptian reception room. Joseph, the recognisable clean-shaven grown man with dark curls from the governor reference, wearing the same white linen and gold-and-turquoise collar, embraces his YOUNG ADULT brother Benjamin at centre, cheek close to shoulder, tears of relief and a real tender smile. Benjamin is an adult about twenty-five with a youthful short beard, in travel-worn pale linen, responding with surprise and affection. At left and right two older bearded brothers react with astonishment and tears, one hand over his mouth, another taking a tentative step closer. These are restrained lifelike human emotions, not broad cartoon expressions. The palace's warm stone and blue/gold pillars softly frame them, late-afternoon light illuminates all faces. The embrace is the only dominant action, LARGE and safely inside the frame, no unrelated props, no soldiers or crowds. Warmth, forgiveness and the possibility of a new beginning, no words or subtitles.
